question: Why is summer warmer than winter?

research.claim: Summer is warmer than winter because Earth's axis is tilted by about 23.44 degrees and keeps pointing the same way as Earth orbits the Sun. When a hemisphere leans toward the Sun, the noon Sun stands higher, so each beam of sunlight is spread over less ground, and the days are longer. In Paris (48.86 degrees north) the noon Sun is about 64.6 degrees high at the June solstice and 17.7 degrees at the December solstice, so a beam covers about 2.97 times as much ground in December; days last about 16.0 and 8.0 hours, and the daily sunlight at the top of the atmosphere is about 5.2 times larger in June, distance included. Earth is nearest the Sun in early January, which changes sunlight by only about 7 percent and works against the northern seasons.
research.explanation: The noon Sun's height above the horizon is 90 degrees minus the difference between the latitude and the Sun's declination, which is +23.44 degrees at the June solstice and -23.44 at the December one. A beam of fixed width arriving at height e covers ground in proportion to 1/sin(e), so the same sunlight is spread thinner when the Sun is low. Day length follows from the sunrise hour angle h0, with cos h0 = -tan(latitude) tan(declination), and the daily total on level ground at the top of the atmosphere is proportional to (h0 sin(latitude) sin(declination) + cos(latitude) cos(declination) sin(h0)) divided by the square of the Earth-Sun distance. Earth's distance ranges from about 147.1 million km in early January to 152.1 million km in early July, a ratio whose square is about 1.069, so distance changes sunlight by about 7 percent, far less than the tilt does.
assumptions: Paris at 48.86 degrees north, at the solstices.
Sunlight at the top of the atmosphere, before air and clouds dim it.
Earth-Sun distance at the solstices about 1.0167 AU in June and 0.9837 AU in December.
research.prediction: At 48.86 degrees north the June noon Sun is 64.6 degrees high and the December one 17.7 degrees; daily sunlight is about five times larger in June.
research.falsifier: If seasons came from distance, both hemispheres would have summer together, in January, which they do not.
limitations: Air, clouds and seasonal lag change the temperatures actually felt; the model covers sunlight only.
The orbit is drawn as nearly round, as it is; its slight oval shape is not visible at this size.
misconceptions: Summer happens because Earth is closer to the Sun.
The tilt makes one hemisphere physically closer to the Sun, and that is what warms it.

sources.title: Season (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: Seasons come from Earth's tilted axis, not its distance from the Sun; the low winter Sun spreads its rays over a larger area; Earth is nearest in January and farthest in July, opposing northern seasons; the distance effect is about a 7% variation in sunlight; seasonal lag makes June to August the warmest northern months; southern seasons are opposite.

sources.title: Axial tilt (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: Earth's axial tilt is about 23.44 degrees, and over an orbit the axis keeps the same orientation relative to the background stars; it moves slowly through axial precession.

sources.title: Apsis (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: Earth reaches perihelion in early January, about 14 days after the December solstice, at about 147,100,000 km, and aphelion in early July at about 152,087,000 km.

sources.title: Daytime (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: Day length varies with latitude and season because of the axial tilt; at the equator it stays about 12 hours in every season; summer days are longer than 12 hours and winter days shorter.

sources.title: Solar irradiance (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: Sunlight on a level surface at the top of the atmosphere scales with the cosine of the Sun's zenith angle and the inverse square of distance; the sunrise hour angle obeys cos h0 = -tan(latitude) tan(declination); the daily total is proportional to h0 sin(latitude) sin(declination) + cos(latitude) cos(declination) sin(h0); losses in the air depend on the Sun's elevation.

scene.title: Why is summer warmer than winter?
scene.subtitle: Earth is nearest the Sun in early January, in the north's winter. So what really makes summer warm?
scene.why: Many people guess summer comes when Earth is nearest the Sun. But Earth is nearest in January, so something else must make summer warm.
scene.opening: Why is summer warmer than winter?

beats.title: Nearest in January
beats.body: Imagine Earth on its yearly trip around the Sun, on a nearly round path. Many people think summer comes when Earth is nearest the Sun. But Earth is nearest in early January, midwinter in Europe and North America.

beats.title: A world with no tilt
beats.body: Imagine Earth spinning like a top, round an upright line called its axis. Each day's spin carries Paris round this circle: half in light, half in shadow. All year, Paris would get 12 hours of light a day: almost no seasons.

beats.title: Tilt it
beats.body: Now tilt the axis 23 degrees, as Earth's axis really is. In June the north tilts toward the Sun, so more of the circle is lit: 16 hours. Half a year later, across the Sun, the same tilt points the north away: 8 hours.

beats.title: A higher Sun
beats.body: Imagine noon in Paris: a Sun straight overhead would stand 90 degrees high. In June the north tilts toward the Sun, so the noon Sun stands 65 degrees high. In December, with the north tilted away, the noon Sun climbs only 18 degrees.

beats.title: Spread-out light
beats.body: Shine a torch straight down, then at a slant: its spot grows and dims. Low in December, the same beam spreads over three times the ground. Spread-out light and shorter days leave Paris only a fifth of June's sunlight.

beats.title: Opposite seasons
beats.body: In December the north tilts away from the Sun, and the south tilts toward it. So in December, Australia has summer while Paris has winter. Nearest in January, Earth gets 7 percent more sunlight: tiny next to the tilt.

scene.takeaway: Summer is warm because your half of Earth is tilted toward the Sun: the Sun climbs higher, its light spreads less, and it stays up longer. Without the tilt, there would be almost no seasons.

questions.q: Isn't tilted toward the Sun the same as facing it?
questions.a: No. Facing the Sun is day and night: as Earth spins, a place like Paris turns to face the Sun once a day, in summer and winter alike. Tilted toward the Sun lasts for months: the whole northern half stays tipped toward it, so its noon Sun is higher and its days are longer. Near the North Pole, the tilt even keeps it facing the Sun all day in June, and turned away all day in December.

questions.q: Then why is July hotter than June?
questions.a: Land and sea take weeks to warm up, so the warmest months come after the longest day. This delay is called seasonal lag.

questions.q: Does Earth's distance matter at all?
questions.a: A little. Earth's orbit is almost a circle: its distance from the Sun changes by only about 3 percent, so its sunlight changes by about 7 percent. Being nearest in January works against the north's seasons, not with them.

questions.q: What would a world with no tilt be like?
questions.a: Paris would get 12 hours of daylight every day, and the noon Sun would stand about 41 degrees high all year. Only the 7 percent change in sunlight from Earth's distance would remain, warming the whole Earth a little in January, both halves at once.

questions.q: Why a fifth, and not a sixth?
questions.a: Three times is the noon figure, and twice the hours counts every June hour as if the Sun were as high as at noon. But June's extra hours come early and late, when the Sun is low, so they add less. And Earth is nearer the Sun in December, which gives December about 7 percent more. So December gets about a fifth of June's sunlight, not a sixth.

questions.q: Does the axis ever move?
questions.a: Over a year, hardly at all. A spinning Earth keeps its axis pointing one way, as a spinning wheel or gyroscope does, so the axis stays aimed at the same stars. Over very long times it slowly swings round, a motion called axial precession.

questions.q: What about places near the equator?
questions.a: There the noon Sun is high all year and days last about 12 hours in every season, so the seasons are mild.

questions.q: Are these sunlight numbers measured on the ground?
questions.a: They count sunlight at the top of the air. Air and clouds dim it on the way down, and more so for a low Sun, which makes winter's share smaller still.

provenance.intro_note: This investigation was made in a coding session, not by the daily run: an AI coding agent built the picture and wrote the guide from sources retrieved in that session, and AI reviewers checked it with the render checks, an accuracy review, a visual review, a first-time-reader test with a subtitle edit, and a blind-viewer test. The owner approved publishing guides made this way. The reviews below are from that session’s final review. Later that day, at the owner’s request, “leans” became “tilted” throughout, and the guide now explains the difference between facing the Sun (day and night) and being tilted toward it (the seasons), in chapter 5 and a new first question. That revision was checked again by an accuracy review and a first-time-reader test. Then, at the owner’s request, the tilt was drawn more intuitively: Earth became a globe drawn from 3D geometry with its axis as a rod, chapter 5 shows Paris’s daily circle lit for 16 hours in June and 8 in December, and after playback the viewer can drag Earth around the Sun or change the tilt. That revision passed the checks and four reviews again. Later, at the owner’s request, the guide was rebuilt in a coding session around the tilt: chapter 2 shows an upright Earth, where Paris gets 12 hours of daylight all year, and chapter 3 tilts the axis 23 degrees, so Paris’s daylight grows to 16 hours in June and shrinks to 8 in December. After playback the viewer tilts the axis by a knob on its north end and drags Earth around the Sun. The pictures were also laid out afresh for every screen size. The rebuild passed the render checks and, after three review rounds, all four reviews; the final reviewers’ copy edits were then applied to the text.

scene.title: Why is summer warmer than winter?
scene.subtitle: Earth is nearest the Sun in early January, in the north's winter. So what really makes summer warm?
scene.why: Many people guess summer comes when Earth is nearest the Sun. But Earth is nearest in January, so something else must make summer warm.
scene.opening: Why is summer warmer than winter?

beats.title: Nearest in January
beats.body: Imagine Earth on its yearly trip around the Sun, on a nearly round path. Many people think summer comes when Earth is nearest the Sun. But Earth is nearest in early January, midwinter in Europe and North America.

beats.title: A world with no tilt
beats.body: Imagine Earth spinning like a top, round an upright line called its axis. Each day's spin carries Paris round this circle: half in light, half in shadow. All year, Paris would get 12 hours of light a day: almost no seasons.

beats.title: Tilt it
beats.body: Now tilt the axis 23 degrees, as Earth's axis really is. In June the north tilts toward the Sun, so more of the circle is lit: 16 hours. Half a year later, across the Sun, the same tilt points the north away: 8 hours.

beats.title: A higher Sun
beats.body: Imagine noon in Paris: a Sun straight overhead would stand 90 degrees high. In June the north tilts toward the Sun, so the noon Sun stands 65 degrees high. In December, with the north tilted away, the noon Sun climbs only 18 degrees.

beats.title: Spread-out light
beats.body: Shine a torch straight down, then at a slant: its spot grows and dims. Low in December, the same beam spreads over three times the ground. Spread-out light and shorter days leave Paris only a fifth of June's sunlight.

beats.title: Opposite seasons
beats.body: In December the north tilts away from the Sun, and the south tilts toward it. So in December, Australia has summer while Paris has winter. Nearest in January, Earth gets 7 percent more sunlight: tiny next to the tilt.

scene.takeaway: Summer is warm because your half of Earth is tilted toward the Sun: the Sun climbs higher, its light spreads less, and it stays up longer. Without the tilt, there would be almost no seasons.

questions.q: Isn't tilted toward the Sun the same as facing it?
questions.a: No. Facing the Sun is day and night: as Earth spins, a place like Paris turns to face the Sun once a day, in summer and winter alike. Tilted toward the Sun lasts for months: the whole northern half stays tipped toward it, so its noon Sun is higher and its days are longer. Near the North Pole, the tilt even keeps it facing the Sun all day in June, and turned away all day in December.

questions.q: Then why is July hotter than June?
questions.a: Land and sea take weeks to warm up, so the warmest months come after the longest day. This delay is called seasonal lag.

questions.q: Does Earth's distance matter at all?
questions.a: A little. Earth's orbit is almost a circle: its distance from the Sun changes by only about 3 percent, so its sunlight changes by about 7 percent. Being nearest in January works against the north's seasons, not with them.

questions.q: What would a world with no tilt be like?
questions.a: Paris would get 12 hours of daylight every day, and the noon Sun would stand about 41 degrees high all year. Only the 7 percent change in sunlight from Earth's distance would remain, warming the whole Earth a little in January, both halves at once.

questions.q: Why a fifth, and not a sixth?
questions.a: Three times is the noon figure, and twice the hours counts every June hour as if the Sun were as high as at noon. But June's extra hours come early and late, when the Sun is low, so they add less. And Earth is nearer the Sun in December, which gives December about 7 percent more. So December gets about a fifth of June's sunlight, not a sixth.

questions.q: Does the axis ever move?
questions.a: Over a year, hardly at all. A spinning Earth keeps its axis pointing one way, as a spinning wheel or gyroscope does, so the axis stays aimed at the same stars. Over very long times it slowly swings round, a motion called axial precession.

questions.q: What about places near the equator?
questions.a: There the noon Sun is high all year and days last about 12 hours in every season, so the seasons are mild.

questions.q: Are these sunlight numbers measured on the ground?
questions.a: They count sunlight at the top of the air. Air and clouds dim it on the way down, and more so for a low Sun, which makes winter's share smaller still.

physics_review.summary: Round 3 accuracy review of the rebuilt seasons guide (se6-scene.json, web/physics.js, web/scene.js, se4-research.json, se6 frames, probes, sizes, plus my own captures and a node harness in /tmp/se6-review-accuracy/). I found nothing wrong in the text or the pictures. Physics.allChecks() runs 241 checks with no failures; the seasons set passes 9 of 9, including the new no-tilt check. Every number matches the model and the research record. The noon Sun stands 64.58 and 17.70 degrees (65 and 18). A beam spreads over 2.97 times the ground (three times). Paris's daylight is 15.97 and 8.03 hours (16 and 8). With no tilt the day is 12 hours and the noon Sun 41.14 degrees. June gets 5.15 times December's sunlight with distance included (5.50 without, 5.9 for the naive 3 x 2), so December gets 0.194, a fifth and not a sixth, and the FAQ's reason for that is right. The distances 147.1 and 152.1 million km differ by 3.4%, which gives 6.9% more sunlight ('7% more than July'); at the solstices the factor is 1.068 ('about 7 percent more' for December). Gold share against the caption: I ran the drawing at 13 stage sizes, every 0.05 s of chapters 2 and 3, and on a live grid of 101 tilts by 151 orbit positions. The lit share times 24 always stays within 0.17 h of dayHours, which is one segment of the 144-segment ring. Both come from the same f and tilt, and the layout only changes the view angle, which the globes share with the orbit. Month names: seasonMonth has no boundary errors against the calendar (assuming Earth moves at an even pace), and the model's day lengths are within 0.12 h of the real Sun-centre day length on every date. The only differences are within about two days of the September equinox, where for example late September shows 11 hours because of rounding. The axis is one 3D vector shared by the orbit Earth, the faint June Earth and the close-up. It leans toward the June Sun and stays parallel in every frame and size. Spin and orbit both turn counterclockwise seen from the north, and the knob drag inverts the projection correctly. Chapter 4 opens with a faint Sun straight overhead on a dashed vertical line marked 90°. The 65° Sun fades in from 7.04 to 7.64 s (the second sentence starts at 7.34 s), and the swing to 18° runs 13.59 to 15.19 s (the third sentence starts at 13.89 s); the drawn angles measure 64.7 and 17.6 degrees. In chapter 5 the beam swings from 6.50 to 8.30 s (the second sentence starts at 6.70 s), and 'covers 3 times the ground' appears at about 7.95 s; the patches measure 58 px and 171 px. In chapter 6 Earth goes June to December and then on to January with the third sentence, and the dots and labels come in on their sentences. The live tag is the rounded tilt actually drawn: settled at 0.47° it says 'no tilt', 0.70° gives 'tilted 1 degree' and 11.95° gives 'tilted 12 degrees' (June 14 hours, November 10, both correct).

learner_review.summary: 1. In my words: Earth spins round an axis that leans 23 degrees and keeps pointing the same way all year. In June the north end leans toward the Sun, so Paris spends more of each daily turn in light (16 hours), the noon Sun stands high (65 degrees) and each beam lands on a small, bright patch. Half a year later Earth is on the far side of the Sun and the same lean points the north away: 8 hours, an 18-degree noon Sun, light spread over three times the ground, about a fifth of June's sunlight. Australia gets the reverse at the same time. Being nearest the Sun in January adds only 7 percent. With no lean, Paris would get 12 hours of daylight every day and almost no seasons. 2. The comparison clicks at frame 6 (and d-c3-dec). It repeats frame 4's layout (June ghost on the left, December on the right, the inset in the corner), but now both axes lean the same way and the readout says 8 hours instead of 12. Watching the axis tip while the readout climbs from 12 to 16 (d-c3-back, d-c3-tilt, frame 5) sets it up, and the yellow part of Paris's ring growing and shrinking shows why. 3. Yes, I want to try it. The white knob on the N end and the small arrows on the path beside Earth show what to grab, and the hint names the readout to watch. The tag ('tilted 23 degrees', 'tilted 12 degrees', 'no tilt') helps: it confirms what the knob did and links the live view back to chapters 2 and 3. 4. I did not get lost. The one step I took on trust is chapter 4's 'so the noon Sun stands 65 degrees high': nothing shows why leaning toward the Sun raises it. Smaller hitches: on short wide screens the opening path is drawn 3 to 4 times wider than tall, right under 'a nearly round path'. In the live view the September inset globe looks almost all dark (we see its night side) while it reads 12 hours. 5. FAQ, answered first from the pictures and subtitles alone. Tilted vs facing: facing is the daily turn into daylight, the lean lasts months; matched. July hotter than June: heat keeps building after the longest day; matched (seasonal lag). Distance: a little, 7 percent, small next to the tilt's fivefold effect; matched, though the step from 3 to 7 percent is not explained. No tilt: 12 hours of daylight all year, with only the distance effect left; matched, and the 41 degrees was new. A fifth, not a sixth: I guessed the distance effect and the low early and late hours; partly matched, and its second clause is hard to follow. Axis moving: it keeps its direction over the year, as frame 6 shows; matched, and precession was new. Equator: I could only guess (about 12 hours all year, mild seasons); matched. Measured on the ground: I guessed the numbers were calculated before air and clouds; matched. 6. Every subtitle meets the rules (80 characters or fewer, one idea, terms defined, no other guides). I propose three small edits. 'midwinter' is the standard spelling. 'as Earth's really is' can be heard as 'Earth is really is'. In the noon opener, 'where' ties the 90-degree scale to Paris, and '90 degrees high' matches the next line's '65 degrees high'. Notes: the June 65-degree noon moment is not in the supplied captures, so I rendered it (with a few other moments) to /tmp/se6-review/shots, and it reads well. The sticky header in the live captures shows the capture page's example title ('Light takes the natural path...'). I treated it as a capture artifact, because the real page (mobile-overview.png) shows this guide's title.
changes: Chapter 4 (A higher Sun): show why the tilt raises the noon Sun. A faint marker at the no-tilt height, 41 degrees (the FAQ's figure), would let the viewer see the June Sun stand about 23 degrees above it and the December Sun about 23 degrees below it, which is the tilt itself. As it is, 'so the noon Sun stands 65 degrees high' is only asserted.

Opening orbit on short wide screens: at 1366x650 the path is drawn about 4 times wider than tall (about 3 times at 1280x700), right under 'a nearly round path', and it looks like the stretched orbit the guide argues against. Keeping the oval at least about half as tall as it is wide would match the words.
Page intro (the why text): 'so something else must warm the summer' reads oddly; 'so something else must make summer warm' says it plainly.

FAQ 'Why a fifth, and not a sixth?': the clause 'twice the hours counts every June hour as if the Sun were as high as at noon' is hard to follow. Suggested opening: 'Three times the ground at noon and twice the hours would make a sixth. But June's extra hours come early and late, when the Sun is low, so they add less.' The rest can stay.
FAQ 'What would a world with no tilt be like?': 'Every day in Paris would last 12 hours' sounds as if a day were 12 hours long; 'Paris would get 12 hours of daylight every day' matches chapter 2.

FAQ 'Does Earth's distance matter at all?': write '3 percent' and '7 percent', as the rest of the text does. Also spell out 'works against the north's seasons, not with them', for example 'so it makes the north's winters, and its summers, a little milder.'
FAQ 'Does the axis ever move?': give the time scale, 'Over about 26,000 years it slowly swings round', instead of 'Over very long times'.

On phones and short screens (390x844-live-mar, 1366x650-live-mar) the page's sticky header covers it. Drawing the path a little lower, or keeping the header off the stage, would keep the knob reachable all year.

blind_review.summary: Pictures 1-12. (1) Space view on a dark navy panel. A glowing yellow 'Sun' sits at the centre of a large slanted orbit ellipse, and a small blue 'Earth' is on the near (bottom) side, showing only a thin lit crescent toward the Sun. (2) Earth has moved to the right end, lit on its Sun side and tagged 'January: 147 million km'. A dashed ghost circle at the left end is tagged 'July: 152 million km'. So Earth is nearest in January, and the two distances look, and are, almost the same. (3) Earth is at the left end with an upright white axis (N on top) and the tag 'imagine no tilt'. A bottom-left inset titled 'June' zooms in on the globe: the Sun-facing half is lit, a circle near the top (Paris's path as Earth spins) is yellow along its lit half, and the caption reads 'Paris's daylight: 12 hours'. (4) The June Earth fades to a ghost tagged 'June', and an upright Earth at the right end is tagged 'December'. The inset, now 'December', is lit from the other side and still says 12 hours, with a grey dot (Paris) on the circle. With no tilt, June and December are the same. (5) Back at June, the axis now leans its N end toward the Sun ('tilted 23 degrees'). In the inset the Paris circle is tipped so about two thirds of it is in sunlight: 16 hours. (6) At December the axis still points the same way in space (parallel to the faded June axis), so the N end now leans away from the Sun. The inset shows a short yellow arc: 8 hours. (7) Cut to the ground in Paris: blue sky, green grass and the Eiffel Tower tagged 'Paris'. An empty dashed Sun outline sits straight above the tower, with a dotted vertical line and '90°', as a reference for straight overhead. (8) 'December noon': the sky is greyer and the grass duller. The Sun is low on the right, with a dashed sight line to the tower's foot and an arc marking 18°. (9) Blue June sky with the Sun high. A pale beam as wide as the Sun lands on a small bright orange strip, 'June patch'. (10) Grey December sky. The low Sun's beam, the same width, slants in and lands on a long, duller strip, 'December patch', with the June patch drawn as a dashed outline inside it and the tag 'covers 3 times the ground'. (11) Back in space: the tilted Earth alone at the December spot, with no tags. (12) Earth has moved a little further, to the January spot of picture 2. Two dots are tagged 'Paris: winter' (north) and 'Australia: summer' (south), plus 'nearest: 7% more than July'. Main idea: seasons come from Earth's 23-degree tilt, not from its distance to the Sun. Because the axis keeps pointing the same way while Earth circles, Paris leans toward the Sun in June and away from it in December. In June that means 16-hour days and a high noon Sun with concentrated light. In December it means 8-hour days and a noon Sun only 18° up, so the same light is spread over three times the ground. With no tilt every day would be 12 hours. Earth is actually nearest the Sun in January, yet that is winter in Paris and summer in Australia. All the numbers I could check from the drawings agree with each other: the January and July spots sit about 13° past the solstice spots, the June Sun is about 64° up, and the patch ratio is about 3. Pictures 13-15 (play): the same orbit and inset. Earth's axis now has a white round knob on its N tip, and two small arrowheads on the orbit, one on each side of Earth, point both ways along it. From 13 to 14, Earth moves from December to June: the tag changes and the inset goes from 8 to 16 hours. From 14 to 15, the axis is stood upright: the tag changes from 'tilted 23 degrees' to 'no tilt' and the inset shows 12 hours. So the viewer can drag Earth around its orbit to pick the month, and drag the knob to change the tilt, and watch Paris's daylight update. The knob, which looks like a handle, and the orbit arrows are the cues. Unclear spots: (a) what the 90° frame refers to (it can suggest the June Sun is overhead in Paris); (b) '7% more' does not say more of what; (c) the inset's circle, yellow arc and grey dot have to be worked out; (d) the slanted orbit looks stretched; (e) in the play view the orbit arrows collide with the ends of the axis.
changes: Picture 7: make the 90° frame say what it is. Tag the empty Sun 'straight overhead' (or similar) and put a right-angle mark at the tower's foot, like the 18° arc in picture 8. Avoid the bright June sky here: an empty Sun straight above Paris on a summer-blue sky lets a viewer conclude the June Sun is overhead in Paris, which it never is.
Picture 9: give the June Sun its angle as well, with a 'June noon' tag like picture 8's and an arc at about 64°. Then the viewer compares June's 64° with December's 18°, not 90° with 18°.

Picture 12: say what the 7% is, e.g. 'nearest: 7% more sunlight' or '7% more sunlight than July'. As written it can be read as 7% closer, which does not match the 147 and 152 million km in picture 2. Naming the month (January) would also help, since this spot is only a little past the December spot of picture 11.

Insets (pictures 3 to 6): tag the grey dot 'Paris' the first time it appears, and show it in picture 3 too (it is missing there but present in 4 and 6). Then the viewer knows the top circle is Paris's daily path and the yellow arc is the part of it in daylight.

Picture 10: the dashed June outline is faint (thin white dashes on orange), and its 'June patch' tag floats in the beam above the ground. Strengthen the outline and keep the tag close to it. 'covers 3 times the ground' would read better as 'spread over 3 times the ground'. A clearer drop in brightness from the June patch to the December patch would show 'same light, spread thinner'.

Orbit (pictures 1, 2, 11, 12 and the play view): the slanted circle reads as a stretched ellipse. In picture 1, Earth on the near side looks much closer to the Sun than it does at the ends, which can feed the very distance idea the guide refutes, and the orbit in the play view is flatter still. A depth cue (the far side of the orbit fainter, or Earth slightly smaller there) or a rounder ellipse would make it read as a circle seen at a slant.

In 14 the upper arrow sits on the axis just below the knob, so the axis itself looks like an arrow, and the orbit line runs through the 'N'. Slightly larger arrows would make it easier to discover that Earth can be dragged along the orbit.

Play view captures 14 and 15 show an orange bar at the top-left edge, and the top of the stage is cut off. Check that these are page or capture artifacts and not part of the picture. The inset caption is small at this size.
